| Point of difference | Railways | Roadways |
|---|---|---|
| Where the journey begins and ends | Transportation is done from one station to another station only. | The vehicle can go along the road right up to the place where the passengers or the goods are wanted. |
| Cost of carrying freight | Carrying freight by railways is cheaper. | The freight transport by trucks is costlier than railways. |
| Fuel and pollution | When railways are used for a part of the distance, the cost of fuel and the pollution caused by trucks are reduced. | Trucks running over the whole distance use more fuel and cause more pollution. |
| Scale of freight movement | A goods train carries many loaded trucks together over the long part of the journey. | Freight transport is carried out on a large scale on the national highways. |
| Working together | In the RoRo (Roll-on Roll-off) system the loaded trucks are carried to the desired station by a goods train. | From that station the trucks take the goods ahead to the desired locations. |

Because of these differences the two are used together in the RoRo transport system, which was used for the first time in India on the Konkan railway.

| Point of difference | Transportation | Communication |
|---|---|---|
| What is carried | Passengers and freight are carried from one place to another. | Information or messages are exchanged from one place to another. |
| Means used | Roadways, railways, waterways, airways and pipelines. | Postal services, newspapers, telephones and mobiles, television, the internet and man-made satellites. |
| Movement | The person or the goods themselves travel over the route. | Nothing is physically shifted; only the message reaches the other person. |
| Points to be considered | Distance, duration, routes and means, cost, time, products, climate, market and physiography have to be considered while choosing the means and the route. | Man-made satellites make it possible to send messages, watch programmes and get information at the same time. |

Both are alike in one important way: transportation and communication are both basic infrastructure, and their development is an indicator of the development of a country or a region.

| Point of difference | Conventional means of communication | Modern means of communication |
|---|---|---|
| Examples | Postal services, such as speed post, and newspapers. | Mobiles, television, the internet and social media, and man-made satellites. |
| How the message travels | The message is written or printed and has to be carried physically to the receiver. | The message is sent through man-made satellites, so it can reach the receiver at the same moment. |
| Number of persons reached at a time | The message is sent to one receiver, or a printed copy has to be given to each reader. | Through video-conferencing we can talk to many people at a time, and a satellite sends the same programme to everybody together. |
| Kinds of work done | Mainly the sending of letters, articles and news. | Besides talking and sending messages, video calling, online trading, payments, money transfer and paying of bills are possible through apps such as the BHIM app and SBI Anywhere. |
| Threats | The chapter does not mention any threat of this kind for them. | A few threats are associated with them, such as website or email hacking, fraud, theft, attack, wars and terrorism, so precautions must be taken while using social networks. |

[Note: the chapter does not give a list of conventional means of communication. It names postal services as a conventional means in the exercise, and Figure 11.5 shows a newspaper stall; the rest of the conventional means known to you are not named in this chapter.]

Communication means the exchange of information, and it is an important process in today's era. A newspaper does exactly this work. The news, articles and pictures collected by the newspaper office are printed and the same information then reaches thousands of readers. Figure 11.5 in this chapter shows a newspaper stall, from where readers buy the paper every day, and such stalls show how widely the newspaper is spread. The newspaper is a conventional means of communication, because the information is printed on paper and the copies have to be physically carried and delivered to the readers. Even so, it reaches many people at one time, which is what a means of communication is expected to do. A reader can keep the paper and read the information again, which is not possible with a message that is only spoken. Like transportation, communication is a basic infrastructure, and the newspaper is one of the means through which this infrastructure works. For all these reasons it is correct to say that newspapers are used for communication.

[Note: the chapter's text does not describe newspapers; it refers to them only through Figure 11.5, the picture of a newspaper stall, so the explanation above is built on the chapter's general statements about communication.]

In today's modern age man-made satellites are an important and effective means of communication, and watching programmes on T.V. is possible through these satellites. The same programme sent by the satellite is received by a very large number of homes at the same moment. Because one broadcast serves so many viewers together, the expense of sending the information is shared by all of them and the cost for each viewer becomes very small. A television set is bought once, and after that the members of the whole family, and often the neighbours also, watch it together, so a single set serves many people. There is no separate charge for each message, as there is when a letter is posted or a journey is made. Through T.V. we get updated information regarding climatic conditions and other news along with entertainment, so a single cheap means gives many kinds of information. The viewer also does not have to travel anywhere to receive the information, so time and money are saved. In this way T.V. is a cheap means of communication.

[Note: the chapter does not state the price of a television set and does not compare the cost of T.V. with the cost of other means of communication; it only states that watching programmes on T.V. is possible through man-made satellites.]

Many types of communication can be carried out through mobiles. The exchange of messages through mobiles is possible with the help of man-made satellites, and Figure 11.3 shows the mobile tower through which this service reaches us. Besides talking on the telephone and sending messages, video calling is available now, so we can see the person we are speaking to. Through video-conferencing we can talk to many people at a time. Mobiles also give us the internet and social media, which everyone needs to use in this age. Many apps which can be used on mobile phones have been developed, for example the BHIM app and SBI Anywhere, and through these we can pay various bills, sell, buy and carry out such transactions. The government of India is incentivising the use of online trading, payments and money transfer, and all of these can be done through a mobile. Updated information regarding climatic conditions can also be obtained through it. While using these facilities we should remember the threats such as hacking, fraud and theft of information, and we should not put sensitive or personal information on social networking sites.

Speed post is the service named in this chapter. Postal services are a conventional means of communication, and speed post is the service through which a letter or a parcel is carried quickly to the receiver. Figure 11.4 of the chapter shows the GPO at Mumbai, that is the main post office of the city, from which such services are given.

[Note: speed post is the only postal service named in the chapter. The other services you may know of at a post office are not mentioned anywhere in this chapter, so the rest of this list has to be completed by visiting or enquiring at the post office near you.]

This question is about your own area, so the answer will be different for every student and it has to be found out by you. Take a road map of your district, or the map of main roads of the kind shown in this chapter for the Satara district, and find the roads marked as National Highways. Write down the number and the name of each highway that passes near your village or town, and also note the two cities that it joins. The chapter names one National Highway, the Nagpur-Surat National Highway, which it mentions while discussing the large-scale production of vegetables at Nandurbar that is not fetching a good price. The chapter also says that a National Highway and a railway route pass through the central part of the Satara district, and that many road networks connect that highway, which is why the transport network of the central part of that district is dense. Freight transport is carried out on a large scale on national highways, so the highway near your area is likely to be busy with trucks.

[Note: the chapter names only the Nagpur-Surat National Highway. The National Highway passing through the Satara district is mentioned but not named, and no highway numbers are given anywhere in the chapter, so the highways of your own area have to be taken from a map.]

| Group 'A' | Group 'B' | Group 'C' | The relation in the chain |
|---|---|---|---|
| Postal services | Conventional means of communication | Speed post | Postal service is the old, that is the conventional, way of exchanging information, and speed post is one of the services given by it. |
| Shivneri | Roadways | Comfortable journey | Shivneri travels on the road, so it belongs to roadways, and when a good means and route are chosen the travelling becomes comfortable. |
| Internet | World network of connected computers | Exchange of information | The internet is a world-wide network of computers joined together, and through it information is exchanged, which is the very meaning of communication. |
| RoRo transport | Railways | Energy, time and labour saving | In RoRo transport the loaded trucks are carried to the desired station by a goods train, so railways are used for a part of the distance and the cost of transport, the fuel and the pollution are all reduced. |

[Note: the chapter does not describe Shivneri anywhere in its text. It appears only in this exercise, and it is placed with roadways because postal services, the internet and RoRo transport already take the other three entries of Group 'B'.]
